“The Udzungwa National Park has not been affected by human activity during the last 20 year, but the buffer zone and connecting corridors have suffered a lot from human impact.

the UMNP is a protected area with high conservation value and that the anthropogenic pressure is mainly located outside the park and in the connecting corridors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a methodology that can support the monitoring of land cover dynamics and the assessment of habitat pressures for protected areas in the long-term.
a novel and integrated approach to assess habitat pressures and values for protected areas, which can be easily replicated for any other protected areas worldwide.
the assessment of land use/land cover change and its impact on protected areas, which is of high interest for conservation management and policy making.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the UMNP is well protected, but the connecting corridors are not.

the UMNP and its surrounding areas have been relatively well preserved, although the buffer zones have suffered a significant loss in the natural vegetation area and a significant gain in agricultural and urban land use.

the UMNP is still in a relatively good condition, but that the surrounding buffer zone and the corridors between UMNP, Ruaha National Park and the Selous Game Reserve are under strong pressure and require urgent attention.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the integration of land use data, habitat data and habitat similarity maps can support the monitoring of the status and the assessment of potential pressures and threats for protected areas and their buffer zones.
we have developed a method and a toolbox for assessing the status and monitoring trends of land cover change in and around protected area and its potential impact to habitats and wildlife.
the UMNP is still in a good status and that it has the potential to become a flagship protected area for wildlife migration and connectivity in East Africa.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the integration of LULCC data with habitat information provides a useful framework for assessing the status of habitats within and surrounding protected areas and for monitoring the trends of habitat changes and pressures.

the integration of LULCC data with habitat information can provide a powerful tool for assessing habitat pressures, which can be used to support decision makers and managers in the conservation of biodiversity and the maintenance of ecosystem services.

the combination of freely available satellite imagery, ecological habitat information and land use/cover information can be an effective tool to assess and monitor the status of protected areas and their surrounding areas and to detect potential threats.
